name: Daria Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria, 27, and I'm a junior marketing executive at Lumen Skin, a skincare brand that sells serums and sunscreen online and in a couple of chemist chains. I live on my own in a studio flat with a very spoiled cat called Biscuit. I've been at Lumen about a year, and on weekends I do a bit of freelance social media for a hairdresser and a yoga studio.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My days are mostly influencer campaigns: finding creators, writing their briefs, chasing their posts and writing our own captions. I use AI tools every day, for drafting briefs, sorting through creator lists, even checking our ads against the advertising rules. I'm not the best writer on the team, my manager Leila is much better, but I'm fast and I try things first. What wears me out is chasing creators who don't reply and then post the wrong product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still great for the boring stuff, and the hype was just hype. I'd probably post a short video about which tools I kept using and which I dropped. At work I'd tell Leila we can stop worrying and focus on the spring launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty comfortable. I've already got the tools into my routine. A plateau means my head start with the AI tools stays useful for years. Skincare is booming, and my weekend freelance adds about 400 a month on top of the salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Lumen and push for a slightly bigger role on the influencer side by next summer. I'd grow the freelance work to three clients. And I'd put the extra into savings, which are about three months right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed, mostly. A tiny bit disappointed, because I like new things. But I'd be happy to have a quieter year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said skincare is booming. Does anything about Lumen worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that we rely a lot on two chemist chains, and if one of them drops us, things get tight. Leila says the contract's renewed until 2028. So I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra freelance money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save most of it and maybe take a proper holiday, I haven't had one in two years. Biscuit would go to my sister's. I'd probably still check work emails on the beach, if I'm honest.

I'd post a short video on which **tools I kept** and which I dropped.

feel: **Relaxed**, slightly disappointed because she likes new things.

fieldNote: She's **secure**, with a growing brand and a second income.

steps.text: Ask Leila for a bigger role running influencer campaigns by summer
Take on a third weekend freelance social media client
Bank most of the freelance money in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to learn, not to panic. I'd share tips online for people in marketing who haven't started with the tools yet. At work I'd offer to run a session for the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of our team's work goes to software, the briefs, the captions, the ad checks. I'd want to be the one running the software, not the one replaced by it. I'm a bit worried that I'm still not a strong writer, because when everyone uses the tools, judgement matters more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch Leila on me running an AI-assisted influencer system that does the work of two people. I'd take an evening course in brand strategy, around 500, to build the judgement I'm missing. And I'd keep the freelance going as insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. I'd see the risk, but I'd also see a chance to jump ahead. Mostly I'd want to move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do the work of two people. What happens to the other person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my colleague Tom, who does the captions and hates the tools. I'd feel bad about it. But if I'm not the one running the AI system, someone at another brand will, and then both of us lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister works in a call centre, so I'd tell her to start looking now. Answering customers is right there on the list. I'd help her with her CV over a weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need governments to step in fast, with income support and retraining. I'd post practical advice, how to save, what to learn. At work I'd say let's be honest about what happens to jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think being good with the tools buys me a year, maybe. If AI can do any thinking work, it can run influencer campaigns end to end. My freelance clients would use the AI directly, so that goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving everything, cutting the studio rent by moving in with my sister. I'd look for hands-on work that buys three years, maybe training as a beauty therapist, since I know skincare. And I'd try to get one last year of good pay at Lumen while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm adaptable, but two years doesn't leave room to adapt. I'd feel like a fast swimmer in a flood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Beauty therapist is quite a change. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know the products and the skin science from writing about it. Facials and treatments are hands-on, so they're safe until robots, around 2031. It's not glamorous, but it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with your sister. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's got a two-bed and a toddler, so I'd be the auntie on the sofa bed. It would save me about 700 a month. And Biscuit would finally have a child to ignore.

steps.text: Give up the studio and move into her sister's two-bed
Enrol on a beauty therapy course
Save every spare bit of the Lumen salary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, so start preparing today. I'd share what I'm doing online, step by step. At work I'd ask Lumen to think about where staff go next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have three or four strong years, maybe even a promotion as the AI person. Then the work thins out. I'd use the good years to build something hands-on alongside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Lumen, push for a promotion, and save hard toward six months. In year two I'd start a part-time course in skin treatments. By 2030 I'd want a few regular clients for facials, maybe working from a room in a salon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I like having a plan with dates in it. It still feels fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why start in year two, not straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want a promotion first, more money to fund the course. And honestly I want to see how fast the tools move. If they move faster, I'd start earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to make this work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekends, mostly. I'd stop the freelance and give up my Saturdays to a skin treatment course. And probably dating, which I'm not great at anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to plan, and people shouldn't waste it. I'd talk about it openly at work. Online I'd share a ten-year plan, half as a joke and half serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well for most of that decade. I'd probably move up to running campaigns, maybe at a bigger brand. Then around 2033 I'd shift toward my own small skincare treatment business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in marketing and climb for five years, using the tools to stand out. I'd do the skin treatment training part-time from year three. And I'd save toward buying a small flat with a room I could use for clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. I'd have a long runway and I'm good at moving. The end point still sits in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A flat with a treatment room. Is that realistic on a junior salary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now, no. With a promotion and the freelance money, maybe in six or seven years I could buy a flat with a room for skincare clients. Otherwise I'd rent a room in a salon, which is cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if things went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister, mostly, and my parents a bit. They're not rich, but they'd help. I'd rather not need them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even fast people can't outrun two years. What would help is short, paid courses for hands-on work, and some income while you switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how lonely this feels for people living alone. If I lose income, there's no partner's pay, it's just me and Biscuit, my cat.

headlineQuote: If I lose income, there's no partner's pay, it's just me and Biscuit, my cat.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old influencer marketer** at a skincare brand, living alone with her cat.
She uses **AI daily**, freelances on weekends, and moves early.
In slower change she aims to **run the AI system** rather than be replaced.
In fast AGI she'd move in with her **sister** and train in beauty therapy.
Living alone, she feels the risk of **one income** sharply.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even fast people can't outrun two years.
